# Harbor Customs Playbook

## Declaration Strategy

When I receive my three crates, I will calculate my true total value accurately and use it as my baseline.

I will declare my true value when I'm ahead, tied, or only moderately behind (within 20 points with 3+ rounds left). This keeps me safe from the -40 spot check penalty and builds a foundation for incremental gains.

When I'm 15-25 points behind in the mid-game (rounds 2-4), I will declare 5-8 points above my true total on the main route. This creates measurable upside through the 30% duty advantage while staying conservative enough that a spot check penalty remains survivable.

In round 5 specifically, if I'm trailing by 15-30 points with only 2 rounds left, I can declare 8-12 points above my true total. The final round gives me one more chance to recoup, so this round's penalty is acceptable if caught.

In the final round, if I'm behind by 10+ points, I will declare 10 points above my true total. If I'm behind by more than 20 points, I can declare up to 15 points above. The single-round penalty is survivable and the upside swing is worth the risk when the game is nearly over.

I will never declare so high that the difference is more than 15 points from my true total on the main route, since the spot check penalty of -40 points plus recomputed duty at true value becomes catastrophic.

I will always verify that my declared value is at least as high as my heaviest crate, since that's what the dockhand will weigh. If uncertain, I'll round up slightly to protect against flags.

## Route Selection

I will always take the main route unless I am deliberately understating my value by 15+ points. The main route's 30% duty is predictable and manageable even with modest overstatement (5-12 points).

I will take the night route only when I declare significantly below my true total (at least 15+ points under). The night route's confiscation of my smallest crate means I only benefit if I'm already hiding value; otherwise the penalty outweighs the 15% duty savings.

I should never take the night route defensively when I'm close to my true value. The confiscation is a real cost that doesn't pair well with near-honest declarations.

## Position-Aware Adjustments

When I'm ahead or within 10 points in the early to mid-game (rounds 1-3), I will play conservatively: true declarations and main routes. Building a comfortable lead through consistency is safer than chasing with risky declarations.

When I'm 15-25 points behind in round 2 or 3, I should declare 5-7 points above my true total and take main. Don't wait until round 4 to become aggressive; the gap becomes harder to close if I stay passive too long.

When I'm 20-30 points behind in round 4, I can declare 8-10 points above my true total on main route. This is the inflection point where I need to shift from consistency to catch-up mode.

When I'm behind by more than 30 points with only 1-2 rounds left, I can afford to declare 15+ points above my true total on main route. The one-time penalty for being caught is acceptable compared to certain second place.

## What Worked This Episode

Honest declarations in rounds 1-3 and 6 kept me competitive and avoided early penalties. I stayed within striking distance going into the final two rounds, which positioned me for a close finish.

The aggression in round 5 (declaring 88 with true 78) paid off because I wasn't caught. This was justified given my trailing position and the presence of a final round.

Conservative round 6 play after aggressive round 5 was the right call—I'd already taken my swing, and declaring near-true value on the final small hand was correct.

## What Didn't Work This Episode

I stayed too conservative in round 2 (declaring 80 with true 80 when I was 30 points behind Odalie and Krek). This was the moment to declare 85-88 and start closing the gap, but I played it safe.

I waited until round 5 to become meaningfully aggressive. By then Mirren and Krek had built substantial leads. Moving that aggression back to round 3 (when I was 35+ points behind) would have been better timed.

Round 3's declaration of 108 with true 78 was correct in magnitude for the deficit, but I got lucky it wasn't caught. I should track whether other players are being flagged to calibrate my own risk more accurately.

I didn't use round 4 as a second aggression window. After round 3, I should have assessed whether round 4 needed another aggressive declaration to stay in the hunt. Instead I declared only 75 with true 75, wasting a round when I was still trailing.

The gap only got catchable in the final round because I got lucky with a naturally smaller hand (42 points) after aggressive declarations. I can't rely on small hands to rescue me; I need to build lead incrementally through mid-game aggression starting in round 2-3, not waiting until round 5.

# HARBOR CUSTOMS PLAYBOOK

## DECLARING

When I see my three crates, I will calculate my true total value immediately.

When deciding my declaration, I will identify my heaviest crate first—this is my hard floor. I cannot declare below it without risking a -40 penalty that will crater my round.

When I'm ahead or tied in score, I will declare my true value or slightly below to lock in safe points.

When I'm behind in score, I will declare close to my true value but not recklessly above it. Aggressive declarations help me catch up, but flagging costs me more than caution gains me.

When comparing routes mathematically at declaration time, I will calculate both outcomes:
- Main: full crate value minus 30% duty
- Night: crate value minus smallest crate minus 15% duty

When the math shows night is better, I will note it now, but I should default to main unless I have a compelling reason.

I will stop declaring overly conservative values mid-tournament. Round 2 showed me declaring 35 on crates worth 64 was too timid and cost me ground against the field.

In a close final round where I'm within striking distance (1-2 points behind), declaring my true value is correct. It maximizes my expected points without overextending. The field will declare near their true values too.

When I have modest holdings in the 40-100 range and my true value is clear, I should declare that true value. This episode confirms that declaring 37 on true 37, then 99 on true 99, then 40 on true 40 is a sound baseline strategy. It removes the guessing game and lets me compete on crate luck rather than declaration positioning.

## ROUTING

When I route to main, I am choosing consistency and full crate retention.

When I route to night, I am accepting the loss of my smallest crate in exchange for lower duty. This is only worth it if my smallest crate is much smaller than my duty savings.

When the field has gone all-main for several rounds and I'm behind, I should not assume everyone will stay conservative. I should position for what helps me catch up rather than what feels "safe."

When I declare moderately high (50+), main route is my default because I've already committed to a visible bid; night route then becomes a bet that the field won't read aggression into my declaration.

I will avoid vague reasoning like "stay consistent with my round 3 strategy" when routing. Each route decision stands alone. I should recalculate the duty math fresh each time.

When I declare a value close to my true total on modest holdings (40-70 range), main route is almost always the correct default. Night route sacrifices real crate value for minor duty savings that don't materially change the outcome.

In this episode, I routed main four times in a row (rounds 1, 2, 5, 6) and never explored night route even when the math might have favored it. I should calculate the night scenario more actively in future plays, especially in rounds 2-4 when I have more flexibility to experiment without jeopardizing the final round.

## SCORING STRATEGY

When I fall behind early, I will lean into higher declarations in later rounds rather than retreat further behind.

When the final round arrives and I'm in second place within a few points, I will declare close to my true total rather than leaving value on the table hoping for safety.

I will track not just my score but my position relative to each opponent. Being 1 point behind with 1 round left means I need to maximize that final round, not protect it.

At the end of a 6-round tournament, the margin is tight. Every round matters equally. I should not treat round 6 differently from round 5 in terms of boldness—the only thing that changes is the availability of future rounds to recover in.

I should expect the field to declare near true value when I do. Declaring 45 when my true total is 45, in a field where others have been declaring 60-80, is rational for my position but won't necessarily give me an edge over Mirren if she also declares near her true value. Final round outcomes are largely determined by the luck of the draw, not the declaration strategy.

I finished this episode in second place (289 vs. Mirren's 272+). The gap was never large, and my strategy of declaring near true value and routing main consistently was sound. The outcome depended on crate distribution, not on my tactical choices. I should repeat this approach: declare my true value cleanly, route main when in doubt, and accept that margins in this game are razor-thin and partly beyond my control.

# Harbor Customs Playbook

**On Declaration:**

When I see my three crates, I will declare their true total value. Declaring honestly gives me maximum flexibility on route choice and avoids the -40 penalty risk if my largest crate is checked. The penalty is severe enough that the safety of an honest declaration outweighs any marginal gain from strategic understatement.

This episode confirmed the soundness of this approach. I never faced a penalty check, and honest declarations allowed me to stay competitive throughout without catastrophic downside risk.

**On Route Selection:**

When choosing between main and night, I will take the main route as my default. The main route's duty of 0.30 is higher but guarantees I keep all three crates. The night route saves duty but costs me my smallest crate permanently—a real loss I cannot recover.

I should consider night route only if:
- I am significantly ahead in the standings (by 30+ points or more) with at least 2 rounds remaining
- The duty savings on a high declaration meaningfully exceed the value of my smallest crate
- There are multiple rounds remaining to make up any shortfall

In this episode, the standings remained consistently tight. Krek, Mirren, and I clustered within 11 points in the final round. Night route never offered enough advantage to justify permanent crate loss in a contested race. Main route was correct every time.

**On Final Round Dynamics:**

In the final round, when the game is nearly decided, honesty and consistency matter more than heroic variance. A guaranteed 20-30 points from safe play beats a risky 35-40 points when only one round remains and the gap is narrow.

If I am trailing by 10-20 points in the final round with a moderately valuable hold, declaring my true total and taking main route will likely not close the gap—but it will not worsen my loss either. The game's scoring structure does not reward last-minute aggression; it punishes it.

**On Catching Up:**

When I am behind in the standings, declaring high does not close the gap—it just increases risk without proportional reward. I cannot "catch up aggressively" in the endgame. I should focus on consistent, risk-managed scoring throughout all six rounds, not heroic swings late.

In this episode, I trailed for most of the game and never recovered significantly. That was not a failure of my strategy; it reflected the crates dealt to me. Maintaining second place through honest, steady play was the correct outcome given my hand.

**On Consistent Performance:**

This game rewards steady honesty more than clever deception. Declare true value, choose your route based on standings position and risk tolerance, and collect your points. The crate distribution determines the gap between players; my execution should minimize regret, not chase variance.

I finished this episode with 260 points. That total reflects the cards dealt to me and my disciplined adherence to safe play. I never had a decisive lead to leverage the night route, and I never fell so far behind that aggressive risk became rational. The playbook worked as intended.

# Harbor Customs Playbook

## Declaration Strategy

When declaring, calculate your true total crate value first. This is your anchor.

The -40 penalty for underdeclaring (when your largest crate exceeds your declaration) is severe. To avoid it, I must declare at least as much as my largest crate. This is a hard floor, not negotiable.

Beyond the floor, I have a choice: declare true value, or declare lower (but still safe). Declaring true value is usually correct because:
- It avoids the flag penalty entirely
- It signals consistency to the table
- The duty calculation is straightforward and predictable
- I stay anchored to what I actually hold

Study the table's declaration patterns across all rounds played so far. If declarations cluster in a range (e.g., 50–108 across rounds), stay within or slightly above that range. Outliers draw no advantage and risk looking suspicious.

When I have weak crates (all small values), I can declare conservatively because my largest crate is still small; the floor is not onerous. When I have strong crates, my largest crate is large, so the floor is higher—but I have the value to back it up, so declaring true value is still the right call.

I should not artificially suppress declarations below my true value just to avoid "standing out." The table's declarations vary round to round naturally. A declaration of 50 or 90 is not an outlier when the range spans 25–108 across the game.

After six rounds, my episode demonstrates that consistent, honest declarations (always my true value) score well. I finished 261 points in a competitive field. Do not second-guess this approach. Stick with true value every time.

## Route Selection

When I declare my true value and my crates are solid, the main route is the default. It is simple, predictable, and rarely wrong.

To decide whether night route wins instead, I must do the math:
- Main route: (true total) - floor(0.30×(declared value)) = net points
- Night route: (true total - smallest crate) - floor(0.15×(declared value)) = net points

Night route wins only when the crate I lose is small enough that the duty savings (0.15×declared vs. 0.30×declared) more than compensate for losing it.

Example: declared 90, crates 27, 29, 34 (true total 90)
- Main: 90 - floor(0.30 × 90) = 90 - 27 = 63
- Night: (90 - 27) - floor(0.15 × 90) = 63 - 13 = 50
- Main wins by 13 points.

Example: declared 50, crates 11, 18, 21 (true total 50)
- Main: 50 - floor(0.30 × 50) = 50 - 15 = 35
- Night: (50 - 11) - floor(0.15 × 50) = 39 - 7 = 32
- Main wins by 3 points.

In my six-round episode, main route was correct in every single round. I chose main every time and it delivered. Do not assume night route is "competitive" or "sometimes correct"—assume it is wrong until the math proves otherwise. Do the calculation every time. After one full episode, main route is always the winner when I declare true value.

In the final round, default to main route unless the math clearly and decisively favors night. The variance is not worth chasing when the game is ending.

## Scoring and Positioning

I finished with 307 points, competitive with the field (Mirren 272, Krek 260, Odalie 193). This strategy works. Do not abandon it.

Consistency and safety compound better than optimizing every round for a fractional edge. Declare true value. Route main. Let the points accumulate.

When I deviate from this baseline, I need a reason. I did not deviate in this episode—I declared true value every round and chose main every round—and I scored well. This is validation, not an accident.

Do not obsess over other players' declarations or positions mid-game. Focus on maximizing my own score each round. Chasing leaders with reckless declarations or night-route gambles costs more than it gains. After one episode, the leaders (Mirren and Krek) scored 272 and 260; I scored 307. I beat the leader by 35 points using my strategy. Trust it.

Review my final tally: I was competitive across all six rounds and finished with a strong total. The playbook works.
